facts.fact_text: The organisers opted to picket Tverskaya Square on 27 November 2005 from 2 p.m. to 4 p.m. next to the Dolgorukiy monument.
The organisers expected that up to fifty people would join the picket (пикетирование) at Tverskaya Square.
At the picket at Tverskaya Square, the organisers intended to express their disagreement with the Moscow mayor's office as to the location of the previously planned march and demonstration.
Despite the position of the district authority, the organisers decided to hold a public gathering in Tverskaya Square on 27 November 2005 at 2 p.m.
The Justice of the Peace noted that the first applicant intended to take part in a public event and to express his opinion in relation to issues of general and political interest.
Under Article 31 of the Russian Constitution, citizens have a right of peaceful assembly.
The special security squad proceeded to arrest some participants at the public gathering in Tverskaya Square on 27 November 2005.
The applicants, along with fifty other people, were taken to the Tverskoy police station following the public gathering on 27 November 2005.

On 29 November 2005 the Justice of the Peace delivered judgments finding some of the applicants guilty of a breach of the procedures for public gatherings under Article 20.2 of the Code of Administrative Offences.

On 30 November 2005 the Justice of the Peace delivered judgments finding some of the applicants guilty of a breach of the procedures for public gatherings under Article 20.2 of the Code of Administrative Offences.
The applicants found guilty were ordered to pay a fine of 1,000 Russian roubles (RUB), except for the ninth applicant.
The ninth applicant was ordered to pay a fine of 500 Russian roubles (RUB).

Under sections 5 and 7 of the 2004 Public Gatherings Act in force at the relevant time, the organiser of a public event (except for an event involving one person) was required to inform the competent authority of the event at least ten days in advance.

Under sections 5 and 7 of the 2004 Public Gatherings Act in force at the relevant time, the organiser of a picket (пикетирование) was required to inform the competent authority at least three days in advance.
Under the 2004 Public Gatherings Act, the competent authority was required to notify the organiser if it had a reasoned proposal for another venue and/or timing for the event.
Under section 5 § 5 of the 2004 Public Gatherings Act, the event could not take place if the event organiser and the competent authority had not approved the alternative proposal.
Under Article 20.2 § 2 of the Code of Administrative Offences of 30 December 2001, a violation of the procedure concerning a public gathering is punishable by a fine.
By order no. 1471-RP of 30 December 1998, the Moscow city mayor introduced regulations concerning city-hall parking areas for service vehicles, including on Tverskaya Square.
The district authority's letter of 24 November 2005 referred to the 'security of the participants' as a reason for the suggested change of venue and timing.
The district authority's letter of 24 November 2005 referred to the need to avoid causing obstruction to pedestrians and vehicles as a reason for the suggested change of venue and timing.

Under Article 55 § 3 of the Russian Constitution, the right of peaceful assembly can be limited by a federal statute in so far as it is necessary to protect the constitutional regime, morals, health or rights or interests of others.
In November 2005 the Moscow city administration authorised a public gathering called 'the Right March'.
The 'Right March' was organised by a number of non-governmental organisations including the Movement against Illegal Immigration and the Eurasian Youth Movement.
The declared aim of the 'Right March' was to commemorate the liberation of Moscow from occupation.
The declared aim of the 'Right March' included expressing the participants' dissatisfaction with the flow of immigration into Russia.
The 'Right March' included a parade from the Chistiye Prudy underground station down to Slavyanskaya Square.
A demonstration was held at Slavyanskaya Square as part of the 'Right March'.
The 'Right March' event lasted for some two and a half hours, according to the applicants.
The 'Right March' attracted several thousand people, according to the applicants.
Reportedly, a number of 'Right March' participants shouted 'Russia for Russians, Moscow for Moscovites!'
Reportedly, a number of 'Right March' participants displayed banners with the slogan 'Let's clean the unwelcome guests out of the city!'
Reportedly, a number of 'Right March' participants displayed banners with the slogan 'Chechens, the war is over. It's time to go home!'
Reportedly, a number of 'Right March' participants displayed banners with the slogan 'Russia belongs to us!'
The organisers expected that up to fifty people would join the picket (пикетирование) at Tverskaya Square.
In a letter of 24 November 2005, the district authority suggested that the picket event be held in Tverskaya Zastava Square instead of Tverskaya Square.
In its letter of 24 November 2005, the district authority suggested the picket event run from 2 p.m. to 3 p.m. instead of 2 p.m. to 4 p.m.
The district authority explained in its letter of 24 November 2005 that under a 1998 order the area around the Dolgorukiy monument was restricted to service vehicles of the Moscow mayor's office.
The special security squad allegedly did not give participants time or opportunity to disperse after a verbal order to do so before making arrests.
The Justice of the Peace found that despite police orders, the event participants refused to stop the picket and thus committed a premeditated administrative offence.
The Moscow city mayor's order no. 1471-RP of 30 December 1998 provided for approximately eighty service vehicle parking spaces on Tverskaya Square during weekdays, not Sundays or public holidays.
